result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_laplacian_spectrum()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L24374-L24591){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_laplacian_spectrum( which="smallest", k=None, normalized=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Returns the spectrum of the Laplacian matrix `L = D - A` (or normalized variant). The Laplacian spectrum provides insights into graph connectivity, cuts, and diffusion processes. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [which]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["smallest"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Which eigenvalues to compute. With `"all"`, this is all `n` eigenvalues (`O(n³)`, recommended for `n < 100`). Using `"smallest"` works with the smallest `k` eigenvalues (default `k=6`). The `"largest"` options works with the largest `k` eigenvalues. [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of eigenvalues to compute for `"largest"`/`"smallest"`. Default is `min(6, n-1)` where `n` is the number of nodes. [normalized]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, use normalized Laplacian: `L_norm = D^(-1/2) L D^(-1/2)`. Normalized version has eigenvalues in `[0, 2]` for undirected graphs. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary with keys: - `"values"`: list of eigenvalues (sorted ascending) - `"vectors"`: list of eigenvectors (each as list of floats) - `"algebraic_connectivity"`: `λ₂` (second-smallest eigenvalue, measures how well-connected the graph is; `0` if disconnected) ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If graph is empty or eigenvalue computation fails. ::: ## Common Use Cases {.doc-common-use-cases} - spectral clustering: use Fiedler vector for graph partitioning - community detection: k-way clustering using k eigenvectors - graph cuts: min-cut via spectral relaxation - synchronization: analyze coupled oscillators on networks - diffusion processes: heat kernel and random walks - network robustness: algebraic connectivity as connectivity measure ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Laplacian $L = D - A$ carries the same structural information as the adjacency matrix but organized so that its algebraic properties align with graph connectivity in particularly clean ways. $L$ is always positive semi-definite, so its spectrum is non-negative, and it *always* has a zero eigenvalue whose eigenvector is the constant vector $\mathbf{1}$. The multiplicity of that zero eigenvalue is exactly the number of connected components, so counting near-zero eigenvalues is the direct spectral test for disconnection. The second-smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_2$, called the *algebraic connectivity* or Fiedler value, is positive iff the graph is connected and quantifies expansion through Cheeger's inequality $\tfrac{h^2}{2\Delta} \le \lambda_2 \le 2h$, where $h$ is edge expansion. Its eigenvector (the *Fiedler vector*) partitions the graph into two well-connected halves by sign, minimizing normalized cut weight in the spectral-relaxation sense, and is the workhorse of spectral bisection algorithms. Passing `normalized=True` switches to $L_{\mathrm{norm}} = D^{-1/2} L D^{-1/2}$, whose eigenvalues sit in $[0, 2]$ regardless of degree distribution; a $\lambda = 2$ eigenvalue signals a bipartite component. This variant is standard in normalized-cut clustering because it handles degree-imbalanced graphs (star-plus-clique structures, for instance) far more gracefully than the plain Laplacian. Signature spectra include $K_n \to \{0, n, \ldots, n\}$, the path $P_n \to \{2 - 2\cos(\pi k / n)\}$, the cycle $C_n \to \{2 - 2\cos(2\pi k / n)\}$, and the star $S_n \to \{0, 1, \ldots, 1, n\}$. Computationally, the "all" mode runs the dense $O(n^3)$ eigendecomposition; the iterative $O(k n^2)$ paths for "smallest" or "largest" (Lanczos with restart) are what make working with graphs of tens of thousands of nodes tractable when only a handful of eigenvalues are needed. ## Examples {.doc-examples} **Detecting Disconnected Components** The number of zero eigenvalues in the Laplacian spectrum equals the number of connected components, so a graph made of two separate pieces has exactly two eigenvalues at (or very near) zero: ::: {#6ccd447a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Graph with 2 components g = ec.Graph(directed=False) # Component 1 g.add_node(label="A") g.add_node(label="B") g.add_node(label="C") g.add_edge(source="A", target="B") g.add_edge(source="B", target="C") # Component 2 g.add_node(label="X") g.add_node(label="Y") g.add_edge(source="X", target="Y") spec = g.get_laplacian_spectrum(which="smallest", k=3) # λ₁ = 0 has multiplicity = number of connected components # Returns 2 (the number of components) sum(1 for v in spec['values'] if abs(v) < 1e-6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#b559bab8 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Algebraic connectivity (= 0 means disconnected) spec['algebraic_connectivity'] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` -3.7944693873150776e-17 ``` ::: ::: **Spectral Clustering with Fiedler Vector** The Fiedler vector (the eigenvector for the second-smallest eigenvalue) naturally splits a graph into two clusters based on the sign of each entry -- nodes with the same sign belong to the same community: ::: {#32be0d5f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Two-way spectral clustering g = ec.Graph(directed=False) # Create graph with two communities... for i in range(6): g.add_node(label=f"n{i}") # Dense intra-community edges g.add_edge(source="n0", target="n1") g.add_edge(source="n1", target="n2") g.add_edge(source="n3", target="n4") g.add_edge(source="n4", target="n5") # Sparse inter-community edge g.add_edge(source="n2", target="n3") spec = g.get_laplacian_spectrum(which="smallest", k=3) fiedler_vector = spec['vectors'][1] # Second eigenvector (λ₂) # Partition based on sign of Fiedler vector cluster_1 = [i for i, v in enumerate(fiedler_vector) if v < 0] cluster_2 = [i for i, v in enumerate(fiedler_vector) if v >= 0] # Returns the two clusters found via the Fiedler vector cluster_1, cluster_2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ([2, 3, 4], [0, 1, 5]) ``` ::: ::: **Measuring Graph Expansion** The algebraic connectivity (`λ₂`) bounds how well-connected a graph is: a large value indicates an expander graph that's hard to partition, while a small value signals a bottleneck that's easy to cut: ::: {#700f3dfe .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(6): g.add_node(label=f"n{i}") g.add_edge(source="n0", target="n1") g.add_edge(source="n1", target="n2") g.add_edge(source="n3", target="n4") g.add_edge(source="n4", target="n5") g.add_edge(source="n2", target="n3") # Algebraic connectivity measures expansion spec = g.get_laplacian_spectrum(which="smallest", k=2) # Cheeger inequality: h²/(2Δ) ≤ λ₂ ≤ 2h # where h = edge expansion, Δ = max degree # A small value here reflects the sparse bridge between the two dense halves spec['algebraic_connectivity'] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 0.2679491924311227 ``` ::: ::: **Normalized Laplacian for Weighted Graphs** Normalizing the Laplacian accounts for degree variations and constrains eigenvalues to the range `[0, 2]`, which is useful when edge weights differ substantially: ::: {#a6d8a831 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_node(label="A") g.add_node(label="B") g.add_node(label="C") g.add_edge(source="A", target="B", weight=1.0) g.add_edge(source="B", target="C", weight=2.0) g.add_edge(source="C", target="A", weight=0.5) # Normalized Laplacian accounts for degree variations spec = g.get_laplacian_spectrum(which="all", normalized=True) # Eigenvalues in [0, 2] for undirected graphs # λ = 0 ⟺ connected component, λ = 2 ⟺ bipartite structure spec['values'] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` [2.220446049250313e-16, 1.231258075056715, 1.7687419249432847] ``` ::: ::: **Random Walk and Diffusion Analysis** The algebraic connectivity also governs how fast a random walk mixes on the graph -- larger values mean the walk converges to its steady state more quickly: ::: {#6c3e805a .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(6): g.add_node(label=f"n{i}") g.add_edge(source="n0", target="n1") g.add_edge(source="n1", target="n2") g.add_edge(source="n3", target="n4") g.add_edge(source="n4", target="n5") g.add_edge(source="n2", target="n3") # Laplacian eigenvalues determine diffusion speed spec = g.get_laplacian_spectrum(which="smallest", k=5) # Mixing time ≈ 1 / λ₂ (algebraic connectivity) # Small λ₂ -> slow mixing, large λ₂ -> fast mixing spec['algebraic_connectivity'] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` 0.2679491924311227 ``` ::: :::
